title: Gideon and the Winter
premise: Casper Zhou, a nonbinary pest controller who has spent a lifetime keeping their head down, is hired to clear an infestation from Gideon House, a decaying estate where the mirrors lag one second behind reality—and in that second, something else moves. The house's original owner, Gideon Vane, bound his family into a song that must be sung by a living voice each winter to keep him fed; the 'pests' are the echoes of those who refused. As Casper befriends the last reluctant heir, Marisol Vane, and her found family of caretakers, they realize the house has chosen Casper as the next voice because invisibility makes a perfect vessel. In the climax, Casper learns the song's final verse—which names the singer and erases them—and instead teaches it to the assembled household, splitting the burden across many voices so no single identity is consumed; Gideon starves, the mirrors catch up, and Casper walks out named, seen, and belonging.
about_author: Odile Winterbourne is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who catalogued the belongings of unclaimed estates for eleven years before turning to fiction. They write horror about houses that remember, and live somewhere cold with too many clocks.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: POV Casper. A routine pest complaint at Gideon House: scratching inside the walls, but no droppings, no tracks—only fingerprints on the inside of the windows. Casper takes the job because rent is due, keeping their usual emotional distance. Beat: wary professionalism masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Inside the house, Casper finds handprints pressed into wallpaper from the inside, ascending the staircase like someone climbing out of the walls. The client, Marisol Vane, watches without surprise. Beat: first crack in Casper's practiced detachment—the prints are small, like a child's.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Working at dusk, Casper notices every mirror reflects the room a beat behind—and in that lagged second, the reflection keeps moving after they stop. They tell themselves it's fatigue. Beat: denial curdling into dread as the house notices being noticed.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Casper's coping ritual—counting doors, checking locks—becomes sinister when the house gains a door overnight. Eleven yesterday, twelve today, and no wall has changed. Beat: the horror of losing control over one's own rituals of safety.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. The last Vane heir explains the family curse obliquely: every winter someone must sing, or the walls fill up. She's stayed out of guilt, feeding the house just enough. Beat: two lonely people recognizing each other's survival strategies.

chapters.title: The Caretakers' Table
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Marisol introduces Casper to the informal household—Dee the electrician, old Tomas the gardener—who keep the lights on and the doors counted together. Casper, invited to dinner, doesn't know how to accept kindness. Beat: warmth offered and almost refused.

chapters.title: What the Walls Keep
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. She shows Casper the nursery where the song was written, its score inked directly onto plaster. The verses are lullaby-simple until the last one, which is scratched out. Beat: grief for generations eaten by a bargain made before any of them were born.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Humming absentmindedly while working, Casper hears the house hum back—in harmony, then in unison, then slightly ahead. The pests go quiet, listening. Beat: the trap closing gently, disguised as belonging.

chapters.title: Echoes in the Ductwork
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Investigating the 'infestation,' Casper finds nests built from photographs, letters, and baby teeth—belongings of everyone the house has taken. Among them, a photo of Marisol's mother, mid-song. Beat: compassion hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. She confesses why the house wants Casper: Gideon feeds best on the unseen, and Casper has spent a lifetime making themselves small. The house isn't haunting them—it's courting them. Beat: fury and recognition; Casper's armor named as bait.

chapters.title: Lights On
chapters.summary: POV Dee. The caretaker's chapter: Dee rewires the house nightly because darkness lets the lag spread room to room. She tells Casper the crew once lost a member who sang along. Beat: found family explained as triage—love as a survival tactic.

chapters.title: Twelve Doors
chapters.summary: POV Casper. The twelfth door opens onto a corridor that shouldn't exist, lined with mirrors all lagging further behind—two seconds, three. At the end, something wearing Casper's posture waits politely. Beat: confrontation with the self the house is building.

chapters.title: The Winter Guest
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Through the mirrors, Gideon Vane himself appears—courteous, patient, genuinely fond of his descendants the way a farmer is fond of livestock. He offers Casper permanence: never invisible again, at the price of never being themselves again. Beat: temptation with a real argument.

chapters.title: Refusal, Overheard
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Casper refuses, and the house stops pretending: doors vanish, the heating dies, frost blooms indoors in shapes like lungs. The song starts playing itself through the pipes. Beat: open hostility; the countdown begins.

chapters.title: Learning the Score
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. She and Casper decipher the scratched-out final verse under lamplight: it doesn't banish Gideon—it completes him, naming the singer so thoroughly that nothing else of them remains. Beat: despair, then the germ of an idea—if the verse can name one person, what if it named many?

chapters.title: The Household Decides
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Casper proposes splitting the verse across every voice in the house, diluting the naming until it holds no one. Dee, Tomas, and Marisol each have reasons to refuse—and choose anyway. Beat: found family crystallizing into a deliberate act of courage.

chapters.title: Rehearsal in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV Casper. With the power cut, they rehearse by candlelight while the mirrors lag worse than ever, reflections mouthing corrections. Casper, terrified of singing at all, practices being heard. Beat: intimate dread braided with growing trust.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. The longest night arrives; the walls fill with echoes pressing to be let out, and Gideon offers one final private deal—leave, and he'll spare the others. Marisol, who has always paid alone, nearly accepts. Beat: the cost of old habits of self-sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Climax. At midnight the house sings the first verses itself, trying to pull Casper's voice into the lead. Instead the whole household sings the final verse together, each voice carrying only a fragment of the naming. Gideon unravels, screaming a name no one owns alone. Beat: terror transfigured into collective defiance.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Show
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Dawn. The mirrors reflect in real time now—but briefly show the household as they truly see each other, not as they fear they look. The twelfth door is gone; eleven remain, counted and held. Beat: exhausted wonder; visibility survived.

chapters.title: Spring Assessment
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Weeks later, Casper returns professionally to confirm the house is clear—no prints, no lag, no song. Marisol asks them to stay on retainer. Casper, who once kept doors counted against the world, leaves one unlocked. Beat: quiet joy; identity chosen, not hidden.

chapters.title: Coda: The Song's New Ending
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. She paints over the nursery score with a new final verse written by five hands—one that names no one and welcomes anyone. Somewhere far off, another lagging mirror goes still. Beat: the curse broken not by erasure but by authorship; the family, extended, endures.
